title: Neck Pain with Arm Pain or Tingling: What a Pinched Nerve Means and What to Do
metaDescription: Neck pain with arm pain, tingling or weakness often means a pinched nerve. Learn the causes, what treatment involves, how long it takes and warning signs.
intro: Neck pain that travels down the arm, with tingling or weakness, often means a nerve in the neck is being pinched or irritated. Doctors call this cervical radiculopathy (a pinched nerve in the neck). Most people improve over time without surgery. Treatment usually starts with medicines, then exercises. Injections and surgery are kept for selected patients. New or worsening weakness needs prompt assessment.

sections.heading: What is a pinched nerve in the neck?
sections.body: Nerves leave the spine through small openings between the bones of the neck. If something narrows an opening, the nerve is pressed or irritated and sends pain into the arm. In older adults this is most often age-related wear: discs lose height, dry out and bulge, and small bony growths called bone spurs narrow the openings. In younger people it is usually a slipped (herniated) disc, sometimes after lifting, pulling or twisting, or an injury. Sometimes no cause is found.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms?
sections.body: The pain typically starts in the neck and travels down the arm. It is often sharp or burning. Turning or tilting the head back can make it worse.
bullets: Tingling or pins and needles in the fingers or hand
Numbness in part of the arm or hand
Weakness in the arm, shoulder or hand
Some people feel relief with their hand resting on top of the head

sections.heading: How is it found, and do I need a scan?
sections.body: Your doctor asks about your symptoms and checks the strength, feeling and reflexes in your arms. X-rays show the bones and narrowed openings. An MRI shows the discs and nerves, and nerve tests are sometimes used. Scans are not needed for everyone. Routine imaging is not required, and an MRI is the usual choice if more detail is needed. Nearly half of middle-aged and older people have worn discs or pinched nerves on scans without any symptoms, so the scan must be read together with the examination. Shoulder, elbow, wrist and heart problems can sometimes feel similar.

sections.heading: How long does it take to get better?
sections.body: The majority of people improve over time without surgery. Some improve within days or weeks and others take longer. A regional NHS guide says most people improve within 3 months, but about one in three treated without surgery still has symptoms. The pain can return, but it usually settles again.

sections.heading: What does treatment involve?
sections.body: Our usual approach starts with medicines for pain, such as anti-inflammatory tablets. For severe nerve pain, doctors may prescribe nerve-pain medicines or a short course of steroid tablets. A soft collar may be used briefly, as long-term use can weaken the neck muscles. Once pain eases, physiotherapy exercises build strength and movement. If pain remains, treatments such as ultrasound, short-wave or TENS may be tried for pain relief only; the evidence for them is modest. A steroid injection near the nerve is for selected patients. It can reduce pain and inflammation, possibly long enough for the nerve to recover, but it does not remove the pressure. Surgery is the last step, only if appropriate, and the decision is yours.

sections.heading: When should I ask about surgery?
sections.body: Surgery is considered if symptoms continue after a period of non-surgical treatment. A regional NHS guide suggests a specialist opinion for disabling arm pain lasting over 3 months, pain that has not responded over 6 weeks, or weakness lasting more than 6 weeks. Which operation suits you depends on your symptoms and which nerve is affected. Many people never need it. We explain the options and the risks, and you decide.

sections.heading: Which warning signs need prompt help?
sections.body: See a doctor promptly, without waiting for the usual weeks of treatment, if you notice any of these:
bullets: Weakness in the arm or hand that is getting worse
Trouble with fine tasks such as buttoning clothes, writing or dropping things
Numbness, tingling or weakness spreading into the legs, or difficulty walking
Pain after a serious injury such as a fall or road accident
Fever, unexplained weight loss or pain that is worse at night

faqs.q: Is a pinched nerve in the neck serious?
faqs.a: Usually it is painful but not dangerous, and most people improve. Worsening weakness or clumsy hands are the signs that need prompt attention.
Most people do not. Surgery is considered only when symptoms persist despite other treatment, or when weakness is getting worse.

faqs.q: Can I exercise with arm pain?
faqs.a: Gentle movement is usually fine. Exercises are most useful once pain has settled. Stop anything that sends sharp pain or tingling down the arm.

faqs.q: Should I wear a neck collar?
faqs.a: Only for a short time if advised. Wearing one for long can weaken the neck muscles.

faqs.q: Does an injection fix the problem?
faqs.a: No. It can ease inflammation and pain for a time, giving the nerve a chance to recover, but it does not remove the pressure on the nerve.

faqs.q: Can this feel like a heart or shoulder problem?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Shoulder, elbow, wrist and heart conditions can feel similar, which is why an examination matters. Chest pain needs urgent care.
